units.title: H418/01 The legal system and criminal law

topics.title: Section A: The legal system - Civil courts and dispute resolution

outcomes.text: Describe the jurisdictions of the County Court and the three divisions of the High Court.
Explain pre-trial procedure and the small claims, fast and multi-track allocation.
State the grounds for appealing a civil decision.
Trace civil appeal routes: first appeal from each track, to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division), and from there onward.
Explain how employment tribunals work.
Describe negotiation, mediation, conciliation and arbitration.
Weigh the advantages and disadvantages of civil courts against alternative dispute resolution.

topics.title: Section A: The legal system - Criminal courts and lay people

outcomes.text: Describe the jurisdiction of the Magistrates' Court and Crown Court.
Classify offences as summary, triable either-way or indictable, and explain their pre-trial procedures.
State the grounds for appealing a criminal decision.
Trace appeal routes: Crown Court, case stated to the Queen's Bench Divisional Court, Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) and the UKSC.
State the aims of sentencing in s142 Criminal Justice Act 2003.
Identify factors affecting sentence and the custodial and non-custodial sentences for adults.
Explain the qualifications, selection, appointment and role of lay magistrates and jurors.
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of juries in criminal cases.

topics.title: Section A: The legal system - Legal personnel

outcomes.text: Describe the role of barristers, solicitors and legal executives.
Explain how the legal professions are regulated.
Describe the types of judge and their roles in civil and criminal courts.
Explain the separation of powers and how judicial independence is secured: tenure, immunity from suit and independence from the other state arms and from the case.
Evaluate the judiciary, including the benefits of judicial independence.

topics.title: Section A: The legal system - Access to justice

outcomes.text: Explain government funding through the Legal Aid Agency, with its availability and restrictions in civil and criminal cases.
Describe private funding, conditional fees and advice agencies such as Citizens Advice and law centres.
Evaluate access to justice, including the effect of legal aid budget cuts.

topics.title: Section B: Criminal law - Rules and theory

subtopics.title: Rules and theory of criminal law

outcomes.text: Define crime and identify the sources of criminal law.
Outline the elements of criminal liability and the parties in a criminal case.
Explain the burden of proof, standard of proof and reverse onus.
Explain the aims, purpose and principles of criminal law and the main theories behind it.

topics.title: Section B: Criminal law - General elements of liability

outcomes.text: Distinguish conduct crimes from consequence crimes, and voluntary acts from states of affairs.
Identify the categories of omission that create liability.
Explain involuntariness as a bar to liability.
Apply factual and legal causation and the ways the chain of causation can be broken.
Explain direct and oblique intention.
Explain subjective recklessness, negligence and gross negligence.
Explain strict liability and the methods used to decide whether an offence is strict liability.
Apply transferred malice and coincidence of actus reus and mens rea.

topics.title: Section B: Criminal law - Fatal offences against the person

outcomes.text: Define murder and state its actus reus and mens rea.
Apply the partial defence of loss of control under s54 Coroners and Justice Act 2009.
Apply the partial defence of diminished responsibility under s2(1) Homicide Act 1957 as amended.
State the actus reus and mens rea of unlawful act manslaughter.
State the actus reus and mens rea of gross negligence manslaughter.

topics.title: Section B: Criminal law - Non-fatal offences against the person

outcomes.text: Define assault and battery under s39 Criminal Justice Act 1988.
State the actus reus and mens rea of assault and of battery.
State the actus reus and mens rea of assault occasioning actual bodily harm under s47 OAPA 1861.
State the actus reus and mens rea of wounding or grievous bodily harm under s20 OAPA 1861.
State the actus reus and mens rea of wounding or grievous bodily harm with intent under s18 OAPA 1861.

topics.title: Section B: Criminal law - Offences against property

outcomes.text: Define theft under s1 Theft Act 1968 and state its actus reus and mens rea.
Define robbery under s8 Theft Act 1968 and state its actus reus and mens rea.
Define burglary under s9(1)(a) and s9(1)(b) Theft Act 1968 and state its actus reus and mens rea.

topics.title: Section B: Criminal law - Defences and preliminary offences

outcomes.text: Define insanity, including the M'Naghten rules and the consequences of an insanity verdict.
Distinguish insane from non-insane automatism.
Distinguish voluntary from involuntary intoxication and apply the defence.
Apply self-defence, including reasonable and necessary force.
Apply duress by threats and duress of circumstances and necessity.
Apply consent as a defence and state its main rules.
State the actus reus and mens rea of attempt.
Explain factual and legal impossibility in attempts.

topics.title: Section B: Criminal law - Evaluation

outcomes.text: Evaluate non-fatal offences against the person, using frameworks such as fitness for purpose, fairness and being up to date.
Evaluate the defences of intoxication, self-defence and consent.
Suggest and assess ideas for reform of these areas.

units.title: H418/02 Law making and the law of tort

topics.title: Section A: Law making - Parliamentary law making

outcomes.text: Explain Green and White Papers and the different types of Bill: Public, Private and Private Members'.
Describe the stages of a Bill in the House of Commons and House of Lords, and the role of the Crown.
Outline the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949.
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of the legislative process.

topics.title: Section A: Law making - Delegated legislation

subtopics.title: Types and uses of delegated legislation

outcomes.text: Describe Orders in Council, Statutory Instruments and By-laws, each with an example.
Explain the reasons for using delegated legislation.
Evaluate its advantages and disadvantages.
Explain parliamentary controls: the parent Act, negative and affirmative resolution procedures and committee scrutiny.
Explain judicial review through procedural ultra vires, substantive ultra vires and Wednesbury unreasonableness.
Judge how effective parliamentary and judicial controls are.

topics.title: Section A: Law making - Statutory interpretation

outcomes.text: Explain why statutes need interpretation.
Describe the literal rule, golden rule, mischief rule and purposive approach, with examples.
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each rule and approach.

subtopics.title: Aids and outside influences on interpretation

outcomes.text: Describe intrinsic and extrinsic aids to interpretation, with examples.
Explain how EU law and the Human Rights Act 1998 affect statutory interpretation.

topics.title: Section A: Law making - Judicial precedent

outcomes.text: Explain stare decisis, ratio decidendi and obiter dicta.
Explain the civil and criminal court hierarchies, including the Supreme Court, and their relevance to precedent.
Distinguish binding, persuasive and original precedent.
Explain overruling, reversing and distinguishing, illustrated with cases.
Explain the exceptions to stare decisis: UKSC Practice Directions and the Court of Appeal's Young v Bristol Aeroplane exceptions.
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of precedent.

topics.title: Section A: Law making - Law reform

outcomes.text: Describe political, public opinion, media, pressure group and lobbyist influences on Parliament, with example Acts.
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of these influences.
Explain who the Law Commission are, what they do and how they reform law.
Evaluate law reform by the Law Commission.

topics.title: Section A: Law making - European Union law

outcomes.text: Describe the membership, role and legal functions of the Commission, Parliament, Council and Court of Justice of the EU.
Distinguish treaties, regulations and directives as sources of EU law.
Explain how doctrines from the CJEU and domestic courts extended rights to individuals.
Explain the supremacy of EU law and its effect on Parliamentary sovereignty during UK membership.

topics.title: Section B: The law of tort - Rules and theory

outcomes.text: Outline the aims of tort law and the protected interests in tort.
Identify claimant and defendant, who may be natural or legal persons.
Explain whether fault must be proved, possible defences and the aim of a tort action.
Discuss the 'compensation culture' and the differences between tort and contract, and tort and crime.

topics.title: Section B: The law of tort - Liability in negligence

outcomes.text: Explain Donoghue v Stevenson and the neighbour principle.
Apply the Caparo test and Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire (2018).
Apply the objective standard of the reasonable man.
Weigh the risk factors in deciding whether duty was breached.

subtopics.title: Damage and special types of loss

outcomes.text: Apply factual and legal causation to damage.
Recognise economic loss from negligent misstatement, psychiatric injury and defective products.
Explain the burden and standard of proof and compensation in damages.

topics.title: Section B: The law of tort - Occupiers' liability

outcomes.text: Define a lawful visitor under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957.
Explain the duty owed to lawful visitors, when it is breached and the defences.
Define a trespasser under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984.
Explain the duty owed to trespassers, when it is breached and the defences.

topics.title: Section B: The law of tort - Torts connected to land

outcomes.text: State the elements of private nuisance, who can claim and who can be sued.
Explain what is an unreasonable interference, the defences and the remedies.
Define the tort in Rylands v Fletcher and the requirements for a claim.
State the defences available.

topics.title: Section B: The law of tort - Vicarious liability

outcomes.text: Explain the nature and purpose of vicarious liability.
Apply the tests of employment status, including 'akin to employment' for non-traditional relationships.
Decide whether a tort was committed in the course of employment, including the Salmond test and 'closely connected' torts.

topics.title: Section B: The law of tort - Defences and remedies

outcomes.text: Explain contributory negligence and volenti non fit injuria.
State the defences available and unavailable for private nuisance and Rylands v Fletcher.
Explain the basis of compensatory damages and mitigation of loss.
Explain the concept of an injunction.

topics.title: Section B: The law of tort - Evaluation

outcomes.text: Evaluate liability in negligence, occupiers' liability and vicarious liability.
Judge fairness, balance of competing interests and whether tort achieves its aims, and compare two similar torts.

units.title: H418/03 The nature of law and Human rights

topics.title: Section A: The nature of law - Introduction to the nature of law

subtopics.title: Law, rules and the rule of law

outcomes.text: Distinguish enforceable legal rules and principles from other norms of behaviour.
Distinguish civil from criminal law by procedure, purpose, outcomes and courts.
Outline the development of English law from custom through common law to statute.
Define the rule of law, its core elements and its importance, and evaluate it.

topics.title: Section A: The nature of law - Law and morality

outcomes.text: Define morality and law, and distinguish immoral from illegal acts.
Explain how moral views differ in a pluralist society.
Explain legal positivism and natural law as theories underpinning law.
Describe cases where morality and law have clashed in the courts.
Apply the main arguments of the Devlin-Hart debate to areas and cases.
Evaluate the relationship between law and morality.

topics.title: Section A: The nature of law - Law and justice

outcomes.text: Explain the meaning of justice and its different types within law.
Outline theories of justice affecting how law is conducted.
Evaluate how far the legal system produces just outcomes.

topics.title: Section A: The nature of law - Law and society

outcomes.text: Explain the role of law in shaping society and as formal and informal social control.
Explain consensus, conflict and labelling theories and how they show in the legal system.
Explain the media's role in moral panic as an agent of change.
Distinguish left realism from right realism and their effect on areas of law.
Evaluate law and society.

topics.title: Section B: Human rights law - Rules and theory

outcomes.text: Explain the features and principles of human rights: universality, interdependence, inalienability, indivisibility, dignity and pluralism.
Explain the constitutional theories underpinning human rights: rule of law, democracy and separation of powers.
Explain approaches to interpretation: balancing rights, proportionality and margin of appreciation.

topics.title: Section B: Human rights law - Protection in the UK

subtopics.title: The ECHR and the Human Rights Act

outcomes.text: Explain the Second World War background to the ECHR and the relationship of the ECtHR, Convention and Council of Europe.
Explain the main provisions of the Human Rights Act 1998 and their impact on domestic law.
Explain how devolution settlements for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland guarantee human rights.

topics.title: Section B: Human rights law - Key provisions of the ECHR

outcomes.text: Explain the right to liberty and security under Article 5.
Explain the right to a fair trial under Article 6.
Explain the right to respect for private and family life under Article 8.
Explain freedom of expression under Article 10 and freedom of assembly under Article 11.
Explain that restrictions come from limits in the ECHR articles and from domestic statute and common law.
Define the key terms within the articles.

topics.title: Section B: Human rights law - Human rights and English law

outcomes.text: Explain public order law restricting Articles 10 and 11: breach of the peace, riot, violent disorder, affray and illegal assembly.
Explain police powers of stop and search, arrest and detention under PACE 1984 and the individual's rights.
Explain interception of communications, data and surveillance under RIPA 2000 and the Investigatory Powers Act 2016.
Explain the duty of confidentiality in relation to Articles 8 and 10.
Explain how obscenity, defamation, trespass to land and harassment restrict Articles 10 and 11.

topics.title: Section B: Human rights law - Enforcement

outcomes.text: Explain how domestic courts interpret and apply human rights before and after 2000.
Explain enforcement through judicial review.
Explain the procedure for a case at the ECtHR, its admission criteria and guiding principles.

topics.title: Section B: Human rights law - Evaluation

outcomes.text: Evaluate protections and restrictions under Articles 5, 6, 8, 10 and 11.
Evaluate the Human Rights Act 1998, criticisms of it and the idea of a UK Bill of Rights.
Suggest and assess ideas for reform.

units.title: H418/04 The nature of law and the law of contract

topics.title: Section A: The nature of law - Introduction to the nature of law

outcomes.text: Tell enforceable legal rules and principles apart from social norms and customs.
Explain the links between law, morality and justice.
Compare civil and criminal law in procedure, purpose, outcome and courts.

subtopics.title: Development of English law and the rule of law

outcomes.text: Trace English law from custom to common law to statute law.
Define the rule of law, its core elements and why it matters for justice and human rights.
Evaluate the rule of law.

topics.title: Section A: The nature of law - Law and morality

outcomes.text: Define law and morality and the function of morals.
Describe the diversity of moral views in a pluralist society and the overlap between immoral and illegal acts.
Explain legal positivism and natural law.
Discuss court cases where law and morality have clashed.
Use the Devlin-Hart debate arguments on specific areas and cases.
Evaluate law and morality.

topics.title: Section A: The nature of law - Law and justice

outcomes.text: Explain what justice means and the different kinds within law.
Describe the theories of justice that shape legal practice.
Judge the extent to which the legal system gives just outcomes.

topics.title: Section A: The nature of law - Law and society

outcomes.text: Explain how law shapes society through social control, formal and informal.
Explain how law creates and handles consensus and conflict, using consensus, conflict and labelling theories.
Explain the media's role in creating moral panic.
Explain left and right realism and how they affect particular areas of law.
Evaluate law and society.

topics.title: Section B: The law of contract - Rules and theory

subtopics.title: Rules and theory of contract law

outcomes.text: Identify the parties to a contract, the burden of proof, the sources of contract law and remedies.
Explain the theories behind contract law: freedom of contract, good faith, consumer protection, fault, balance of interests and inequality of bargaining power.

topics.title: Section B: The law of contract - Formation

outcomes.text: Distinguish invitations to treat, bilateral and unilateral offers and counter offers.
Apply the rules on communication of acceptance and revocation of offers.
State and apply the presumption for domestic agreements and when it is rebutted.
State and apply the presumption for commercial agreements and when it is rebutted.
Apply the rules on adequacy and sufficiency of consideration.
Explain past consideration, pre-existing duties and promissory estoppel.
Explain the privity rule and the common law exceptions to it.
Explain third-party rights under the Contract (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999.

topics.title: Section B: The law of contract - Terms

outcomes.text: Explain incorporation of terms and distinguish express from implied terms.
Explain terms implied by common law, statute, course of dealings and the Consumer Rights Act 2015.
Distinguish conditions, warranties and innominate terms.
Explain the term-based and breach-based approaches, their problems and consequences of breach of each type.
Identify when a term will be treated as a condition.
Explain common law regulation of exclusion clauses.
Explain statutory regulation under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 and the Consumer Rights Act 2015.
Explain regulation of exclusion clauses in non-consumer contracts.

topics.title: Section B: The law of contract - Vitiating factors

outcomes.text: Explain fraudulent, negligent and innocent misrepresentation under the Misrepresentation Act 1967, including negligent misstatement.
Explain the remedies for each kind and omission in consumer contexts.
Explain the nature and consequences of the threat, and the extra criteria in Pao On v Lau Yiu Long.
Explain the remedies and limits.

topics.title: Section B: The law of contract - Discharge

outcomes.text: Explain discharge by performance and its exceptions: tender, severable contracts, substantial, partial and delayed performance.
Explain the grounds for frustration, its limits and its financial consequences.
Explain repudiatory and non-repudiatory breach and the damages for each.
Explain breach of a condition, innominate term and warranty.
Explain anticipatory breach and the choices open to the other party.

topics.title: Section B: The law of contract - Remedies

outcomes.text: Explain the basis for a claim in damages, causation and remoteness, and foreseeability of loss.
Explain mitigation of loss and enforceability of liquidated damages clauses.
Explain the equitable remedies of specific performance and injunction.
Explain Consumer Rights Act 2015 remedies: rejection, partial rejection, short-term right to reject, price reduction and repeat performance.

topics.title: Section B: The law of contract - Evaluation

outcomes.text: Evaluate formation rules: offer and acceptance, intention, consideration and privity.
Evaluate incorporation and classification of terms and exclusion clauses.
Suggest and assess ideas for reform.
